summary: A 94-foot stone tower on a rocky island about three miles off Washington, first lit 1 January 1892; keepers, rescues, and a disputed 2008 shutoff.

access.note: Visitation is restricted to protect seabirds and sea mammals; the USLHS record says not open to the public.

visit.note: Site and tower closed (nature preserve); accessible only by boat.

facts.agency: U.S. Coast Guard (owner, until the 2008 shutoff, per the Lighthouse Directory); Quillayute Needles National Wildlife Refuge (site manager)

events.note: Lighthouse Board reserves the island's 30 acres for lighthouse purposes (8 June)
Lighthouse Board asks for and later receives an $85,000 appropriation for a first-order light and fog signal
Bark Cassandra Adams strikes a reef near the island on 10 August; the date is disputed by the Port Townsend Argus
Christian Zauner arrives as head keeper (August)
94-foot dressed stone tower ready for occupancy in November 1891
First-order Fresnel lens by Henri LePaute and Sons (made 1888) placed in the lantern
Fog signal put into operation 1 November 1891 (item 923 text); the report's list of new fog signals dates the siren 15 November 1891
Light exhibited continuously on and after 1 January 1892; Zauner lights the wicks at 4:26 p.m.
Keeper Clifford B. Hermann and assistants Carl Lien and Anders G. Berner aid a schooner in distress on 30 November (year inferred from the fiscal-year 1913 roll)
Keeper Albert Beyer aids the launch Myrtle May; shelter and provisions for crew and passengers
Keeper Albert Beyer and assistants William Hill and Harvey A. Walker care for three men in a disabled launch
Keepers Harry Oakley, Karl Luoma and Jens Pedersen make an unsuccessful attempt on 1 May to rescue two men from a fishing boat wrecked on a reef
Coast Guard absorbs the Lighthouse Service; rotating Coast Guard crews replace resident keepers
Coast Guard proposes closing the light; protests by mariners stop it
Light automated; last resident keepers leave in the early 1970s
Fresnel lens replaced by a solar-powered beacon (VRB-25); lens removed for security
The first-order lens goes on display at the Westport Maritime Museum
Light extinguished in April 2008 (Lighthouse Directory); the USLHS record still shows an active aid

corrections.why: The Light-House Board's report for the year ended June 1892 says the light was exhibited continuously from 1 January 1892, and HistoryLink dates the first lighting to that day. The 1891 date is the year the tower was completed and the fog signal began (sources disagree; the USLHS record gives 1891 as the year established).

The Lighthouse Directory reports the light extinguished in April 2008, and HistoryLink says it has been automated since 1968 with no keepers. The USLHS record still shows an active aid, so a human should check the current Coast Guard status before this is changed.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: Sources give 1891 (USLHS and Wikidata-style records, which take the year the tower was finished) and 1 January 1892 (the Light-House Board's report and HistoryLink, which record the first lighting). The story follows the report and HistoryLink.
The archive's principal-keeper line for Zauner begins in 1889, which matches HistoryLink's account that he arrived in August 1889 while the tower was still being built.

notes_for_editor: Disagreements now stated in the story: (1) first lighting: the Light-House Board's report and HistoryLink give 1 January 1892; the USLHS record and the Lighthouse Directory give 1891 (the year the tower was finished or the station established); (2) fog signal: the 1892 Light-House Board report gives 1 November 1891 in item 923 but 15 November 1891 in its list of new fog signals (scan p. 337); (3) distance: HistoryLink and the 1889 blog say about three miles; the Directory says 3.5 mi (6 km); (4) status: the Directory says extinguished April 2008; the USLHS record still shows an active aid (Yes). Cassandra Adams date: HistoryLink says 10 August 1888 (a Friday). The Puget Sound Weekly Argus of 23 August 1888 has an OCR that reads 'the 16th inst.' and mentions a Thursday; 16 August 1888 was a Thursday. The story says the date is hard to read and gives the reading. CHECK THE PAGE IMAGE before any change (loc.gov sn96061109/1888-08-23 sp=3). Citations: the 1892 report is cited by scan page (581-582, 336-337) because the printed page numbers the OCR head gives (198?, 199?) are unconfirmed. Commissioner 1921 and 1922 passages: scan pages 668 and 756 (archive.org bub_gb_B2dYAAAAYAAJ); the printed pages are not confirmed. Bulletin pages are PDF pages (1914 pp. 2 and 4; 1927 p. 28). The 1914 'fiscal year 1913' label is on PDF p. 2; the Destruction Island list (Nov 30) is on PDF p. 4; the story gives the year 1912 from the fiscal-year label. Names matched in running prose, not by table position: the 1921, 1922 and 1927 keeper names and the 1914 rescue names. The USLHS roster (135 stints: 16 principal, 25 first, 38 second, 42 third, 1 laborer, 13 USCG) was counted and matches the story. The 1927 Bulletin boat name is OCR 'Piol(eer'; the story does not name the boat. HistoryLink is a secondary essay; its primary citations (House Report 1558 of 1882; the 1888 appropriation) were not re-checked. The USCG Historian's page was not used. The island is a closed nature preserve; the story gives no access guidance beyond 'closed' and the view from U.S. 101. Wikipedia is not cited. The Wikipedia lead, if used, is not in the story.
